headline: Japan's Chances Squandered as Sweden Steal Unlikely Draw
story: Japan commanded Dallas with measured intensity, their 3-4-2-1 formation conferring midfield control through Maeda and Suzuki. The 56th-minute goal arrived cleanly: a 0.60 xG opportunity dispatched as it should be. But six minutes later, Sweden's aggressive pressing (4.9 high-press phases against Japan's 3.3) conjured an improbable response—a 0.02 xG goal that defied logic. The narrative inverted: Japan, now chasing, pressed forward while Sweden defended the fortune they'd somehow inherited.

Japan's numerical advantage in quality (1.22 to 0.56 expected goals) masked a clinical deficiency. Three shots on target could have been four; at 83', a gilt-edged 0.31 xG chance was spurned. Sweden's reply relied on volume and luck: 11 shots but only five on target, their 0.56 xG return from possession-light play. Elanga (7.9) orchestrated Sweden's salvage; Maeda (7.7) commanded Japan's attack but could not overcome their wastefulness.

keyMoment.text: Sweden score from 0.02 xG, an improbable equaliser that defies possession and chance creation

points: Clinical finishing: 0.31 xG miss at 83' was the match; score and Japan wins
Defensive discipline: Sweden's 0.02 xG goal shouldn't land; tighten shape on scrambles
Pressing intensity: 3.3 high-press phases vs Sweden's 4.9 surrendered initiative in midfield

away.verdict: Pressing produced fortune, not dominance; efficiency squandered it.
points: Shot quality: 11 shots, 5 on target, 0.56 xG reflects poor decision-making under pressure
Finishing: 0.19 xG miss at 79' would have made Sweden's pressing count
Conversion advantage: One scrambled goal from 4.9 high-press phases reveals underexecution

statLine: Japan's 1.22 expected goals to Sweden's 0.56 tells the story: one team created, the other capitalized on chaos and pressing intensity.
